author: Carlos Martinez
title: Spa-Francorchamps on iRacing: My Corner-by-Corner Notes From the Rig
description: My corner-by-corner notes and setup approach for Spa on iRacing, raced from a MOZA R9 direct-drive rig.

sections.p: I run all of this from a fixed-aluminium-extrusion cockpit with a ~MOZA R9 direct drive wheelbase and ~MOZA CRP2 load-cell pedals — no motion, no fancy paint, just a rig built to be honest about what the car is doing. This week it's Spa — one of the tracks I keep coming back to on iRacing, and one where the corner-by-corner details matter more than most. I've raced enough laps here across enough car classes that I've stopped thinking of it as one lap and started thinking of it as a handful of separate problems strung together, which is honestly how I'd recommend approaching any new track once you're past the total-beginner stage.

None of what follows is a substitute for laps. iRacing's tire model and each car's balance shift enough between builds and seasons that exact setup numbers go stale fast — what doesn't go stale is which corners at Spa punish which mistakes, and that's what I'm actually trying to hand off here.

Before I get into setup or technique, it's worth walking the layout once with fresh eyes, because most of the time lost at a new track comes from not knowing what's coming next rather than from any actual driving mistake.

list: Eau Rouge–Raidillon — a blind, uphill compression that punishes any hint of lift, taken flat in most GT3s once you trust the car
Les Combes — a heavy braking zone after the long Kemmel Straight run, where late-braking mistakes turn into gravel-trap moments
Pouhon — a long double-apex left-hander that rewards commitment and punishes an early throttle stab
Blanchimont — flat in the faster GT cars, terrifying in anything with less downforce
Bus Stop chicane — the final corner before the pit straight, tight and easy to overslow

sections.p: I'd genuinely recommend doing a slow, no-pressure lap or two just looking around before pushing for pace — glance at the runoff, the curbing, and where the track actually widens versus where it only looks like it does. A surprising amount of confidence at Spa comes from simply knowing the track's shape well enough that you're not making decisions on the fly anymore.

sections.h2: Where I set up the car differently here

sections.p: My starting point for Spa is never a totally clean-sheet setup — I take whatever baseline I'm running that week for the car class and adjust from there based on what this specific layout demands.

list: I run slightly less front wing than my baseline Silverstone setup — Spa's long straights reward a bit more top speed
Ride height goes up a touch through Eau Rouge unless the car has real aero underneath it — bottoming out mid-compression is how I lose the rear
Brake bias moves a hair rearward for Les Combes and the Bus Stop, since both are hard, straight-line stops

sections.p: I'd treat all of this as a starting point rather than a final answer. Setup work on iRacing rewards small, deliberate changes tested one at a time far more than it rewards big swings based on a feeling — change one thing, run a handful of laps, and actually compare lap times and how the car felt rather than just going on instinct.

sections.h2: A practice session plan that actually works

olist: Run three or four laps at a moderate pace just to build a mental map of the corners before pushing for time
Push for a genuinely fast lap once the tires and track feel warmed in, and note exactly where you felt like you left time on the table
Adjust one setup parameter based on that feeling, then run another push lap to see if it actually helped
Finish with a longer run at race pace rather than qualifying pace, since that's closer to what you'll actually need on race day

sections.p: Spa's elevation changes show up as real weight transfer through the ~MOZA R9's direct-drive motor — I keep my in-game FFB strength moderate here so the Eau Rouge compression doesn't clip and mask the subtler stuff happening at Pouhon.

I mention wheel feel specifically because Spa is a good example of how much a track's character can change what a 'good' FFB setting even means. A profile that feels great somewhere flat and smooth can feel either numb or harsh somewhere with real elevation change or bumps, and this track is one where I've had to actually revisit my base settings rather than assume they'd transfer.

sections.tip: Spend a session in a slower car (Skip Barber or the MX-5) learning the Spa layout before you bring GT3 speeds to it — the corners don't change, but your margin for error shrinks fast.

sections.h2: Mistakes I still see (and sometimes still make)

list: Lifting through Eau Rouge 'just in case' — it almost always unsettles the car worse than committing
Braking too early into the Bus Stop out of habit from a slower class
Ignoring the blind crest before Les Combes and getting surprised by traffic

sections.p: What all of these mistakes have in common is that they're habits carried over from somewhere else — a different track, a different car, a different session — rather than something specific to Spa itself. The fix isn't usually a dramatic technique change, it's just deliberately unlearning the habit that doesn't apply here.

sections.h2: Race craft specifically at this track

sections.p: Single-lap pace and race pace at Spa aren't the same skill, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I only talked about qualifying laps. In traffic, the corners that felt straightforward in isolation often play out completely differently — a car ahead braking a fraction earlier than you expected, or a car alongside taking away the line you were planning to use. I try to build in a little more margin at the corners I've flagged above specifically because that's where a first-lap mistake compounds into an actual incident rather than just a slow lap.

None of this replaces seat time — track knowledge on iRacing comes from laps, not from reading about them. But knowing where the trouble spots are before you find them the hard way saves a few incident points along the way. If you're still dialing in your braking feel generally, I wrote up my notes on a stable cockpit separately, and it's worth reading alongside anything track-specific.

faqs.q: What's the hardest corner at Spa on iRacing?
faqs.a: Eau Rouge–Raidillon tends to catch the most drivers, based on what I see in replays and incident reports.

faqs.q: Do I need a high-end wheelbase to learn Spa?
faqs.a: No — track knowledge and braking points transfer across wheel setups. A direct drive wheel like my ~MOZA R9 makes the feedback clearer, but it won't teach you the line by itself.

faqs.q: How many laps does it usually take to feel comfortable here?
faqs.a: It varies a lot by driver, but I'd budget a full practice session or two of focused laps before expecting genuine confidence, especially at a technical or blind-corner-heavy track.

faqs.q: Does setup matter more than driving line at this track?
faqs.a: Driving line first, always — a good setup makes a well-driven lap faster, but it won't fix a fundamentally wrong line or braking point.
